claim: The open fields between Seminary Ridge and Cemetery Ridge were used in two Confederate attacks (July 2 and July 3); the field's lack of cover, together with the numerous farmsteads and fence lines that helped break up the Southern formations, resulted in the repulse of both assaults

quote: Occurring in the fields bordered by Seminary Ridge to the west and Cemetery Ridge to the east, this broad plain was seen by the Confederate high command as an ideal avenue of approach, for it allowed rapid movement across it and thus was used during two Confederate attacks (July 2 and July 3) against the Union line on Cemetery Ridge. The field’s lack of cover, however, gave the Union defenders excellent observation and fields of fire over and into it. That, along with the numerous farmsteads and fence lines which helped break up the Southern formations, resulted in the repulse of both assaults.

claim: On the morning of July 1, 1863 the 8th Illinois Cavalry set up a vidette post at the Wisler house and blacksmith shop; at 7:30 am the cavalrymen saw Heth's division advancing and Lt. Marcellus Jones, borrowing Sgt. Levi Shafer's carbine and resting it on one of the Wislers' fence posts, fired the first shot from the western yard
feature: First shot of the battle: 8th Illinois Cavalry vidette at the Wisler house, 7:30 am July 1
quote: On the morning of July 1, 1863, the 8th Illinois Cavalry established a vidette post at the home and blacksmith shop of Ephraim Wisler. From its position on Knoxlyn Ridge, the Wisler House was an ideal location from which to spy any Confederate advance toward Gettysburg down the Chambersburg Pike. At 7:30 am, Union cavalrymen detected the advance on Henry Heth's Confederate division, which had departed their Cashtown bivouac to conduct a reconnaissance in force toward Gettysburg. Lt. Marcellus E. Jones, who commanded the picket line of the 8th Illinois, borrowed the carbine of Sgt. Levi Shafer, rested the weapon on one of the Wisler's fence posts, and from the western yard of the home fired the first shot of the Battle of Gettysburg.
source_author: National Park Service
source_date: web page, undated unless noted; as served 2026-11-13

claim: The post and rail fence along the Trostle-Wigert Lane, which Union forces used to reach battle sites from Taneytown Road, is documented in the 1872 survey and Tipton photographs
feature: Trostle-Wigert Lane fence (Trostle Field 10 south boundary)
quote: The Trostle-Wigert Lane was used by Union forces to reach battle sites and positions from Taneytown Road. This avenue of approach was a significant movement corridor for Union artillery and infantry throughout the last two days of the battle and was defended aggressively to prevent Confederate forces from attaining the Union rear. The fencing likely provided cover to Union forces traveling on the lane. Additionally the fence likely became an obstacle to lateral movement across the lane by both forces during the course of the battle.34 Post and rail fencing is documented in the 1872 topographical survey map and in photographs from the Tipton Collection

claim: The report says that in 1977 the western slope was cleared and livestock introduced, worm fences were built along the roadways to enclose the pasture and the breastworks at the east end of the pasture were converted into stone-rider fences, introducing features that had not existed in July 1863
feature: 1970s pasture: worm fences along the roads and stone-rider fences on the breastworks, features that had not existed in July 1863
quote: control techniques in 1977, the western slope of Little Round Top was cleared and an attempt made to control vegetation through the introduction of livestock. Cows and sheep were pastured in the Plum Run Valley but they proved ineffective at controlling vegetation growth. Worm fences were built along the roadways to enclose the pasture and the breastworks at the east end of the pasture were converted into stone-rider fences, with the result of introducing features into the landscape that were confusing to some visitors and had not existed in July, 1863.

feature: How the park's 1863 base map was made
quote: The eras mapped included: 1863, the battle; 1895, the end of management by the Gettysburg Battlefield Memorial Association; 1927, the end of management by veterans of the Civil War (and just prior to National Park Service management); and 1993, when aerial photography documented the current conditions. A Cultural Landscape Inventory quantified current conditions and was completed in 1996. The information gathered was mapped on base maps at a common scale, and the maps were digitized. By comparing the maps it is possible to see how the battlefield and surrounding areas have changed over the past 135 years, and to estimate the extent of the changes. The maps were based on extensive research. Historians used park archival materials, library records, period photographs, period sketches, maps, and for the 20th century, aerial photographs. Important maps included those developed by Bachelder (1863 and 1872), Warren (1868) and others to document the field at or near the time of the battle, and maps developed by the War Department and NPS to document existing conditions at various periods.

quote: Vegetation Other than crops, the only known vegetation (managed plant material) in the national cemetery site by July 1863 was the Meyers apple orchard, which was described as “an orchard of gnarled old leafy trees,” by one veteran.66 The orchard served as a cover both for infantry and artillery. While older farm orchards of the period often consisted of seed trees scattered across a field, it appears the Meyers orchard, which was probably more of a gentleman’s orchard than a farm orchard, may have followed advances in fruit growing with ample, even spacing of nursery-grown trees, generally about 30 feet apart. The orchard probably included several varieties of apple.

quote: Improvements within the cemetery through June 1863 included hundreds of marble and granite grave monuments, that included piers with urns, obelisks, and tablets, some of which were grouped in family plots surrounded by ornamental iron fences (fig. 1.19). Rocky debris from excavation of graves was dumped within a small circular avenue where the cemetery vault was planned, in an area referred to as the “rocky centre.”41 The road frontage of the cemetery was outfitted with a temporary white-painted wood plank fence and entrance gate, in place of the “tasteful front enclosure”—an ornate iron fence and gate— that the cemetery association hoped to erect (see fig. 1.18). The rest of the grounds were to be enclosed by an Osage orange hedge, a plant with heavy branching and thorns popular for keeping out livestock, although these plans were put on hold as well. By ca. 1860, a water pump at the rear of the gate lodge had been enclosed by a decorative wooden gazebo with lattice walls and a conical roof.
